articles.title: Giant veg Guinness World Records broken at Malvern Autumn Show
articles.summary: Seven records are thought to have been broken at the National Giant Vegetables Championship.
articles.body:
Seven giant vegetables are believed to have smashed Guinness World Records as competitive growers showed off their supersized produce at competition.

The provisional records were set on Friday at the National Giant Vegetables Championship , part of the Malvern Autumn Show at the Three Counties Showground in Worcestershire.

Among the potential record holders was a 26.02kg (4st 1.8lb) beetroot, a 7.808kg (1st 3.2lb) sunflower head and a cucumber plant measuring more than 7.5m (24.6ft).

The achievements came despite a challenging summer for growers, with record-breaker Graham Barratt - who presented the giant cucumber plant - describing the weather as "bonkers".

Organisers said the seven records would need to be verified, with confirmation expected on Saturday.

Barrett said his success had come down to feeding the vegetable the "right things at the right time", but this year's hot and dry weather had made growing more difficult.

"This year, only one word can describe it - bonkers," he said.

"You've had to look after your plants more, you've had to keep them watered, fed... most things have finished too early for the show, so next year I think we have to learn to start the plants a bit later."

According to the provisional results, the record breakers are:

Peter Glazebrook - heaviest sweetcorn kernel - 0.408kg (0.8 lb)

Graham Barratt - tallest cucumber plant - 7.598m (24.6 feet)

Terry King - dandelion/weed with the longest root - 1.127m (3ft 7in)

Vincent Sjodin - heaviest beetroot - 26.02kg (4st 1.8lb)

Vincent Sjodin - heaviest sunflower head - 7.808kg (1st 3.2lb)

Kevin Fortey - longest tromboncino - 1.486m (4ft 8ins)

Kevin Fortey - heaviest luffa - 5.014kg (11.1lb)

'Why we flushed away Dragons' Den investment'

Why council plans to offer buildings to advertisers

Growers have faced unusually difficult conditions this year following a hot and dry summer, with many having to provide significantly more water to their crops.

Steve Harris, who grew a 23.5kg (3st 7lb) marrow, described the process as a "balancing act".

"Giant marrows need about 20 litres (5.2 gallons) a day to help them grow - so it's been a real balancing act to make sure they have enough to continue to thrive, but not so much they actually split," he said.

Derek Hulme, 65, from Stoke-on-Trent, said some giant pumpkin and marrow growers had seen their vegetables split because of the conditions.

"The conditions have been so dry, we're watering more. But then the vegetables soak up more than it can actually cope with and then they split wide open."

Neil Hands, who won the heaviest red cabbage category with an 18kg (2st 12lb) entry, said the heat had also caused problems.

"It's too hot for my cabbages," he said. "They need it to be cooler. I've just been watering and watering."

Despite those conditions, some enormous entries made it to Malvern.

Ian Paton won the heaviest pumpkin category, while Jack Baggs took the heaviest marrow title with a 107kg (16st 12lb) entry and Curtis Leach won the squash category with one weighing 279.5kg (44 st).

Maggie Walter, from Plymouth, took home a £1,000 prize after her 3.95kg (8.7lb) aubergine was judged the heaviest.

She said she "never expected" to win and described the victory as a "nice surprise all round".

Walter grew eight aubergine plants in a polytunnel using irrigation from a borehole, but said several had gone soft when they came to harvest them.

"We parted the foliage a bit more and at the back there was this bad boy," she said of her winning vegetable.

Other winners included Derek Richardson, whose 45.5kg (7st 2lb) swede topped its category, while Sjodin also produced the heaviest kohlrabi at 31.5kg (4st 13lb).

Joe Atherton dominated several categories, growing the heaviest cantaloupe melon and onion, as well as the longest beetroot, carrot and parsnip.

This year's championship attracted 597 entries from 169 growers competing across 33 categories.

Tim Saint, from Reading, Berkshire, entered eight different types of giant vegetable, including a 304kg (47st 12lb) pumpkin.

"I get up at 05:30 in the morning before work and as soon as I get home at 17:00 I'm out again until it's virtually dark," he said.

Despite the work involved, Saint said meeting other growers at Malvern made the effort worthwhile.

"Its like a gathering of the clan really," he said. "Everyone is so nice - it's like meeting your family."

articles.title: Cambridge narrows probe into late professor Jason Arday’s hiring, drops plagiarism focus
articles.summary: The University of Cambridge narrows its investigation into the hiring of Professor Jason Arday, shifting attention away from plagiarism allegations to examine the welfare and support provided to him during his tenure.
articles.body: The University of Cambridge has narrowed its inquiry into the hiring of professor Jason Arday following his death last month, with the review now focusing on whether he received adequate support from the university, NYT reported.Cambridge had announced a broader investigation earlier this summer into Arday's appointment after allegations emerged that he plagiarised parts of his doctoral thesis and embellished aspects of his personal history. Those allegations, along with questions about his academic record, are now outside the main investigation's scope.Arday could still be mentioned in a separate review examining Cambridge's wider hiring and academic misconduct policies, but that inquiry will not focus on his case.The shift comes after Vice Chancellor Deborah Prentice had promised a “thorough and transparent” investigation into Arday's appointment.Nazir Afzal, the former prosecutor appointed to lead the main review, said the inquiry would instead examine Arday's welfare, care and the support available to him.“It’s not about the allegations made against Professor Arday or about his academic record,” Afzal said. “It’s about his welfare, his care, his well-being.”Afzal, who is also chancellor of the University of Manchester, said the inquiry would go “deep on a narrow question rather than broad on all of them”.A separate expert panel will examine the wider context of Arday's time at Cambridge, including policies governing hiring and academic misconduct and the support provided to academics facing intense public and media scrutiny.The decision has divided Cambridge faculty. Some professors are circulating a letter calling for a full examination of Arday's appointment and the university's role in promoting his personal story, according to a draft seen by NYT.Cambridge appointed Arday as a professor in 2022 when he was 37 and promoted him as its youngest Black professor. He had said he could not speak until the age of 11 and could not read until 18. His claims later became part of scrutiny surrounding his biography.A faculty letter issued before Arday's death criticised administrators for “crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential”.Arday's family said he had faced an intense online campaign, describing it as a “campaign of misinformation” that had become too much for him.Some faculty members have also criticised Cambridge's handling of the case before his death, including Prentice's description of it as an “aberration” in a letter to staff.You use AI every day. articles.title: Senior Kazakh officials detained after 14 service members swept out to sea
articles.summary: Seventeen service members were swept out to the Caspian Sea during military exercises.
articles.body:
Five senior military officials have been detained in Kazakhstan following the death of 14 service members who were taking part in military exercises.

Those who died were among a total of 17 who were swept into the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a boat on Thursday. Officials say the incident occurred "during a combat training mission due to a sharp deterioration in meteorological conditions and increasing winds".

Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They are suspected of criminal negligence.

An interior ministry committee has been set up to investigate the incident, which occurred some 43km (27 miles) from the city of Aktau in south-western Kazakstan.

Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said a pretrial investigation into the deaths was being conducted.

The investigation was looking into the decisions made during the organisation and execution of the military training exercise, whether safety requirements had been observed, and weather conditions had been taken into account - in addition to technical specifications of the boat.

More than 500 military personnel, warships and coastal units were participating in the Caspian Defense 2026 military exercise, according to the Kazakh ministry of defence.

articles.title: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside
articles.summary: The identity of the 28-year-old man, who fell down a vertical gully to his death, is yet to be confirmed.
articles.body:
A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain.

The man fell into a gully while descending from the summit of Torrecerredo in the Cantabrian Mountains on Thursday, the Spanish Civil Guard said.

Police and an air unit were deployed to the scene after emergency services were called around 13:27 local time (11:27 GMT). The man's body was recovered by a mountain rescue unit.

The UK Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities "following reports of the death of a British national in Spain".

Spanish emergency services said they initially received a call saying that a person had fallen on the eastern face of the mountain and dispatched a rescue group aboard a medical helicopter.

A doctor among them confirmed the man's death at about 14:18 and remained at the scene to guard the body until a Civil Guard helicopter could arrive about an hour and 20 minutes later.

Specialist mountain rescuers were then lowered by winch to the site of the accident, where they recovered the man's body and belongings.

The identity of the climber, who Spanish authorities said was English, has not been given. The accident occurred when he was about 20 metres from the mountain's summit.

His body has been transported to the Institute of Legal Medicine, which provides forensic pathology services, in Asturias, the Civil Guard said.

Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,650m, is in the Picos de Europa, which is popular with climbers and walkers.

The region's tourism board describes the route up the mountain as "very difficult" with a demanding ascent, warning climbers to take particular care on steep and exposed upper sections on their way down.

Sepa Asturias - the body responsible for emergency services in the region - said it also transported a 54-year-old French woman to hospital after she suffered a leg injury on the mountain range on Thursday afternoon.

articles.title: More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees flee to Chad as UN calls for funding
articles.summary: UN refugee agency says 400 people a day, about 20 times the previous daily rate, now cross from Sudan into eastern Chad.
articles.body:
More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees have fled to neighbouring Chad this year, compounding a humanitarian crisis that will only deteriorate further unless there is a significant increase in funding, the United Nations has warned.

The number of Sudanese people arriving in eastern Chad has “accelerated sharply” over the past week and is outpacing the available support, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, said on Friday.

The number of refugees entering via Chad’s border areas of Adre and Tine has risen to 400 people a day, about 20 times the daily rate of previous months, the agency added.

Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023, when a power struggle between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti, turned violent.

More than three years later, in excess of 11 million Sudanese people have been displaced in what has become the world’s largest displacement and humanitarian crisis.

Approximately 6.4 million people in Sudan are internally displaced, while more than 3.5 million Sudanese refugees and asylum seekers have fled to nearby countries.

The UN warned on Friday that the transit centre in Chad’s Tine is under severe pressure and currently hosts more than 4,300 people, many of whom are in urgent need of shelter, water, sanitation and protection services.

About 31,000 families lack adequate shelter, and most refugees are living on less than half of the minimum amount of water needed daily.

The UN says it has so far received only 20 percent of the $1.6bn needed to fund response efforts. It says that the dire situation will deteriorate further unless the international community helps plug the funding shortfall of $1.28bn.

The UN warned that without additional help, more Sudanese refugees will make the perilous journey to Europe. More than 14,100 Sudanese refugees arrived on the continent last year, a 245 percent increase compared with 2024.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s new rebel alliance faces an old problem
articles.summary: Former enemies have united against Abiy Ahmed, but disputes over territory, power and command could pull them apart.
articles.body:
The formation of a new armed alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed follows a pattern that has plagued Ethiopia – an empire of many nations and nationalities still in the making – for decades. Those in power leave little space for peaceful political struggle; the winner takes it all, so those who feel disadvantaged take up arms to change the status quo. Actors and alliances change over time, but violence remains the only constant.

The civil war in parts of Oromia has raged since Abiy took power in 2018, while the conflict in the Amhara region has raged since 2023. In Tigray, the Pretoria agreement was never fully implemented. Although large-scale war had not resumed, the region had been under siege since a faction of the TPLF took power and escalated its confrontation with the federal government. Until the latest escalation, Abiy’s government had largely been content to control the centre of power while confronting rebels with drones and ground forces.

The government held national elections despite voting not taking place in Tigray and several other districts. It formed the Ethiopian National Dialogue Commission in 2021, which concluded a national conference of about 4,000 participants in August, despite the absence of armed groups and other key opposition organisations. At the same time, the government has continued to pursue major development projects. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was in Djibouti on September 24 for the launch of the Ethiopia-Djibouti petroleum infrastructure project. The newly elected parliament is due to open on October 5, when a new federal government will be constituted.

The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, announced on September 20, was not a surprise. It followed several months of coordination meetings among the groups, held in the presence of military and security representatives from Eritrea and Sudan. It brings together the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and four movements from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Despite the OLA’s participation, Oromo organisations and elites are divided in their support for the alliance. The alliance aims to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and establish an inclusive transition. Three of the seven organisations – the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Afar National Unity Revolutionary Front (ANURF) – have particular strategic importance. All three are in northern Ethiopia, which borders Eritrea, allowing continuous logistical support from there.

Three days later, TPLF forces, allied with the ANURF, advanced into several districts in Zone 2 with little resistance. ANURF is led by Ibrahim Osman Aliyu, known as Haji Ibrahim, a respected figure from Berhale in Zone 2 and a relative of Ethiopia’s defence minister, Aisha Mohammed. He defected to Eritrea last year with a contingent of Afar Special Forces and local forces. In a message to the Afar people, he assured them that the current fighting was directed against the Prosperity Party, not the Afar people or fighter groups, and that services and public transport would continue unhindered. He advised Afar residents to join his forces or stay away from the fighting. Their next target may be the vital highway linking Ethiopia to Djibouti.

We have seen part of this story before, though this time the alliance took longer to form. In November 2021, nine opposition groups hastily announced the United Front of Ethiopian Federalist and Confederalist Forces. Tigrayan forces and the OLA advanced towards Addis Ababa, while the alliance’s leaders spoke of dismantling Abiy’s government and installing a transitional authority. By January 2022, the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front had left the united front, accusing the TPLF of killing Afar civilians. In December of the same year, the Benishangul People’s Liberation Movement signed a peace deal with the regional government. The federal army counterattacked, Tigrayan forces withdrew from neighbouring regions and the TPLF eventually signed the 2022 Pretoria agreement with the government. That pact required the TPLF to stop supporting armed groups elsewhere in Ethiopia.

The same pattern could repeat itself. The lesson is not that 2026 will mirror 2021 exactly. The new alliance includes Fano, whose fighters stood with the federal government against the TPLF during the earlier war and now fight Abiy. The government is also fighting on several fronts. But the precedent shows how quickly a common enemy can stop being enough when battlefield fortunes change.

Both Fano and the TPLF claim western Tigray, or what the Amhara call Wolgait-Tsegede. The founding statement offers no settlement. A Tigrayan leadership that abandons its claim risks alienating people displaced from their homes; a Fano leadership that concedes it risks losing the support of fighters for whom the territory is central. Calling the issue a matter for later negotiations buys time but does not create a compromise. The same problem reaches beyond the north: Oromo, Amhara and Somali movements do not share one vision of Ethiopia’s federal order, boundaries or distribution of power.

Nor does each organisation speak for everyone in the population it claims to represent. Tigray’s leaders are divided over their relationship with Addis Ababa and the Pretoria settlement. Fano is a collection of regional commands with different priorities. Even the Ogaden National Liberation Front’s participation has exposed an internal dispute: An overseas faction supports the alliance, while leaders inside Ethiopia’s Somali region deny joining it. A seven-signature declaration cannot settle these questions of mandate.

Then there is the military problem. These forces operate across distant regions and can stretch the federal army, forcing Addis Ababa to defend multiple theatres. But simultaneous fighting is not the same as a single campaign. A successful march on the capital would require reliable supply routes, coordinated command and political support in the areas through which fighters must pass. Government drones make concentrated formations and exposed supply lines more vulnerable. Air power alone cannot govern contested towns, but neither can an alliance govern them simply by capturing them.

Eritrea adds another risk. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing the alliance; Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar allegations, though ample evidence suggests otherwise. Relations between the two countries have deteriorated sharply amid Ethiopian calls for Red Sea access and disputes left unresolved after the Tigray war. Outside support could strengthen individual factions, but dependence on Eritrea could also make them unacceptable to other Ethiopians. If the Ethiopian government comes to see Eritrea as a direct threat, it may attack, with unpredictable consequences and the risk of drawing in other regional powers. If Abiy’s government itself comes under serious threat, the UAE may become fully involved to rescue one of its closest regional allies.

Three paths now seem possible. The most likely is prolonged, uneven conflict: Local offensives and temporary bargains weaken the government’s reach without dislodging it from Addis Ababa. A second is alliance fragmentation. If western Tigray, Afar or another disputed territory becomes the price of cooperation, some partners may leave or make separate deals. A renegotiation of the Pretoria agreement and concessions from Abiy to Tigray could also take the TPLF out of the alliance, as happened to the ambitions of the 2021 front. A less likely but far more dangerous possibility is a cascade of federal military defections and coordinated rebel advances. Even then, a rebel takeover would constitute an unconstitutional change of government under African Union rules and face regional opposition. Removing Abiy would settle none of the arguments over land, command and constitutional power. Victory could open another civil war.

Ethiopia has repeatedly watched coalitions of convenience promise a new beginning through force. What matters now is not whether an armed alliance or a government survives, but what happens to the people who will have to live with what both do next.

articles.title: How 'largest phone smuggling network' was uncovered by Met
articles.summary: Police say up to 40,000 phones were smuggled - the equivalent of around 40% of devices stolen in London.
articles.body:
It started with a single stolen mobile phone, found inside a sealed parcel, inside a warehouse near Heathrow airport.

It ended in police dismantling what detectives believe to be the UK's largest phone smuggling network.

The device had been electronically tracked to the warehouse not by officers, but by a victim who had it stolen from them just before Christmas in 2024 and alerted the DHL courier company.

"The phone was ringing in the package," explains Commander Andy Featherstone, the Metropolitan police's lead on mobile phone theft.

"It was still on. Which is very unusual in these circumstances, because they tend to be wrapped up, so the signal isn't working. But in this case it was."

Stolen phones are often wrapped in aluminium foil in order to block wireless signals and prevent the devices from being tracked.

When police were called to investigate, they found more than 800 devices, packaged in batches of five, stacked into nine boxes, some wrapped in foil, others in bubble wrap.

All were stolen and they were destined to be shipped to Hong Kong.

A major inquiry known as Operation Echosteep was launched, with detectives who specialise in investigating armed robberies and drug smuggling brought in to track down suspects.

Further shipments were intercepted and officers used forensics on the packages to identify two men, who were placed under surveillance.

In September 2025, police stopped a car being driven through Waltham Forest and arrested Amir Muhammad Khadikhel and Ismat Miakhel.

Inside, they discovered several phones strewn around the back seat, with others on the floor wrapped in foil.

Both men were found wearing necklaces featuring pins to remove the handsets' Sim cards.

Police say about 2,000 more devices were discovered at properties linked to them.

Southwark Crown Court heard that one shop, Roshan Fruit and Nuts, on Lea Bridge Road in Leyton, east London, had been used to store the stolen phones.

Police found a trapdoor, leading to a basement where boxes labelled as containing dried goods held packages of phones wrapped up in foil, as well as £44,665 in cash.

In another property, the court heard stolen phones had been found stored inside the microwave.

Prosecutor Karen Robinson KC said the men had played a "leading role" in a "sophisticated and criminal network" that had seen more than 5,000 phones seized by police, with a value in the UK of around £5.5m.

The court heard Khadikhel had fled Afghanistan in 2019 and travelled to the UK as an asylum seeker.

A third man, Mansoor Mohammed, who came to the UK from India on a visa in 2019, was also identified as being involved in the handling of devices.

Khadikhel, 35, from Wanstead, and Miakhel, 33, from Walthamstow, along with Mohammed, 30, from Wood Green, pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to handle stolen goods and participating in criminal activities of an organised crime group.

Khadikhel and Miakhel also admitted to conspiracy to remove stolen goods.

On Friday, Judge Adam Hiddleston sentenced Khadikhel to nine-and-a-half years' imprisonment, Miakhel to nine years' imprisonment and Mohammed to six-and-a-half years' imprisonment.

The judge said the offending had been on an "enormous scale financially" and the criminality was "highly organised and sophisticated".

The prosecutor added that phone smuggling in London was "prolific" and a "very significant societal problem".

Police suspect the network was responsible for smuggling up to 40,000 phones during 2024 and 2025, exporting them to China. It is the equivalent of around 40% of all devices stolen in London at that time.

Featherstone says that wider group has "many layers in its hierarchy", with handlers recruiting street thieves via social media and advertising how much they were willing to pay them per stolen device.

"So a modern device, or the most recent phone that had been released, would fetch a higher premium - in most cases around the £500 mark," he explains.

"This network were collecting phones all across London from street thieves, and then they would take those phones in, and when they had enough they would then package them up and ship them out of the UK into China."

Saira Pike, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "Phone theft is more than just a financial loss as it involves victims losing personal data, precious pictures or memories and their sense of security.

"Amir Khadikhel, Ismat Miakhel and Mansoor Mohammed were at the heart of a sophisticated organised crime operation that profited from the misery of victims who had their mobile phones stolen across London."

Police say children are often recruited over social media to steal phones.

Featherstone tells me one 14-year-old boy was stopped by officers with around 20 stolen phones on him, something he could potentially receive thousands of pounds for in a single day.

"Some of these devices, particularly iPhones, can fetch up to £5,000 in China and Hong Kong. The reason being that they can work on the internet without any type of restriction," Featherstone said.

"This was a global operation, millions of pounds involved, because of the value of these devices."

The Met says it has made 14 arrests connected to Operation Echosteep, seized more than £250,000 in cash and recovered more than 10,000 stolen phones, though the number of victims reunited with their devices is lower, at more than 1,000.

The number of recorded mobile phone thefts and robberies fell to 62,029 in the year ending August 2026, compared to 78,344 for the same period the previous year - a drop of 20%.

In the borough of Westminster, which has the highest rate of phone theft of any London borough, 672 phone thefts and robberies were recorded last month, the equivalent of around 21 a day.

Featherstone acknowledges the numbers are still "too high", saying: "This is where we need assistance from industry, because this cannot be resolved by arrests and prosecutions and we need assistance from industry to design this problem out."

In June, the Metropolitan police commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he had written to the Home Secretary asking for legislation to make phone companies publish data on stolen devices and whether they are reconnected, and to enforce measures to make stolen devices "unusable bricks".

The force said it had started sharing data with Apple to more closely track whether stolen handsets get reconnected to a phone network after they are taken.

articles.title: MindsEye: Ex-GTA developer's studio faces closure
articles.summary: Build A Rocket Boy, founded by Leslie Benzies, has gone into administration after its debut game flopped.
articles.body:
A video game studio founded by a former senior Grand Theft Auto developer is facing closure 15 months after the disastrous release of its debut game.

Edinburgh-based Build A Rocket Boy (Barb) launched MindsEye in June 2025 to a string of bad reviews and player complaints, with some calling it "the worst game" of the year.

Former workers said development of the game was chaotic and accused its boss, Leslie Benzies, of mismanaging the studio.

Barb has now gone into administration - a process which could result in it being sold to a new owner or closed down.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Barb for a response.

Benzies set up Barb in 2016 - the same year he left Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games after a legal row over unpaid royalties.

It began work on Everywhere, intended to be a multiplayer role-playing game set in a futuristic city, before pivoting its focus to action-adventure MindsEye.

The project attracted a lot of interest and, according to company documents , Barb had managed to attract more than £233m of investment by 2024.

Former staff previously told BBC Newsbeat the development process had "no coherent direction" and accused senior managers of failing to listen to their concerns.

Following the game's turbulent launch, between 250 to 300 members of staff were made redundant.

Shortly before this, during an all-staff call, Benzies alleged "internal and external" forces had conspired to hinder MindsEye's release, and vowed to root out "saboteurs" within the company.

When Newsbeat asked Barb about this, it released a statement saying: "Leslie and the entire senior management team take full responsibility for the initial launch [of MindsEye].

"The version of the game that was released did not reflect the experience our community deserved."

Since its release, the company has failed to attract a bigger audience to the game with a series of fixes and content updates.

After further layoffs, reports last week suggested the remaining workers at the studio had also been let go.

What does going into administration mean?

A company goes into administration when it can no longer pay its bills - referred to as insolvency.

Any payments to creditors - people or companies they owe money - are put on hold while proposals to restructure the business are drawn up.

An administrator from a qualified accountancy firm is put in charge while this process takes place, and one of their main jobs is to keep the business running, usually until a new owner can be found.

They must also make sure creditors are paid back as much money as possible.

This is usually done by selling off assets such as equipment, furnishings and anything else that can be sold to raise cash.

Administration can take months and, in the worst-case scenario, a company can be put into liquidation and shut down if it has no way of making any more cash.

According to Barb's most recent accounts, for the period up to September 2025, it incurred a £36.2m loss and had £10.5m in net assets.

articles.title: Darts set for major 2027 shake-up with new TV major and France hosting ranking event – but what does it mean for Luke Littler?
articles.summary: The PDC European Tour will visit France for the first time next year in Lievin, just a few kilometres from Lens in northern France, as well as the introduction of the European Open; you can watch World Grand Prix Darts live on Sky Sports from September 28 - October 4
articles.body:
A significant addition to the 2027 PDC calendar will see the inaugural European Open take place in Salzburg from June 18-20.

The new three-day event will follow the World Cup of Darts, which returns to Frankfurt from June 10-13, before the sport heads to Blackpool for the World Matchplay from July 17-25.

The introduction of the European Open, which will feature all PDC Tour Card holders competing for a £750,000 prize fund, will increase the number of darts majors from 11 to 12.

That means another challenge for world No 1 Luke Littler in his bid to complete a clean sweep of victories in all of the PDC's premier televised events - a feat achieved only by Michael van Gerwen.

The new major comes after Littler opted to skip several events on the European circuit, while the announcement also follows his threat to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after he was booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals.

The European circuit is also set for a significant expansion, with the European Championship increasing to 48 players across six days of action and £1m in prize money on offer.

The European Tour will visit France for the first time next year, with Lievin set to host the fourth event of the 15-tournament season from March 19-21, on the weekend before the Easter holidays.

The historic trip to France will follow European Tour events in Kiel, Krakow and Riesa, with the circuit also returning to established destinations across Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Belgium, Switzerland, Hungary and the Netherlands throughout 2027.

PDC Chief Executive Matt Porter said the changes reflected the continued growth of darts across Europe and would provide greater opportunities for players at every level of the professional game.

"The continued growth of darts across Europe has been hugely exciting to see, and these developments represent another significant step forward for the PDC circuit.

"The introduction of the European Open, alongside an expanded European Championship and increased prize money across the European Tour, reflects the strength of the sport and our commitment to creating more opportunities for players.

"We're also delighted to be increasing investment in the Challenge and Development Tours, providing greater opportunities and rewards for players throughout the professional pathway.

"2027 promises to be another hugely exciting year for the PDC and we look forward to continuing the sport's growth across Europe and around the world."

The 2027 PDC calendar will get under way with Qualifying Schools in Milton Keynes and Kalkar from January 4-10, before the Winmau World Masters takes place in Milton Keynes from January 27-31.

The Premier League will then begin in Glasgow on February 4, kicking off a 17-night tour across the UK and Europe before Finals Night at The O2 in London on May 27.

The Players Championship circuit will also get under way in February, with 34 events scheduled to take place across the UK and Europe throughout the year.

The European Tour, meanwhile, will begin in Kiel from February 12-14 before breaking new ground with its first-ever visit to France the following month.

Following the World Cup and European Open in June, the World Matchplay will once again take place at Blackpool's Winter Gardens, with the nine-day event concluding on July 25 alongside the Women's World Matchplay.

The European Tour will resume in Leverkusen in July, with further events taking place in Bratislava, Ghent, Basel, Budapest and Maastricht during the second half of the season.

The World Grand Prix will return to Leicester from September 27-October 3, while the European Championship will expand to six days in Dortmund from October 26-31.

The Grand Slam of Darts will then take place in Wolverhampton from November 6-14, before the Players Championship Finals returns to Minehead from November 26-28.

The year will conclude with the World Darts Championship at London's Alexandra Palace in December.

Further changes will also be made to the PDC's Challenge and Development Tours in 2027. Both circuits will be staged across six three-day weekends, with one tournament taking place on each day.

Prize money will increase to £30,000 per event, with prize money paid down to the last 128 players in each event.

Sky Sports remains the home of darts with the World Grand Prix (September 28-October 4), Grand Slam of Darts (November 14-22) and World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) all live. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

articles.title: Mystery solved? Two arrested in connection with NYC’s sewer emergence
articles.summary: Two men were arrested in connection with this week’s mysterious sighting of sewer invaders emerging from a New York City manhole cover, court records revealed on Friday.
articles.body: Two men were arrested in connection with this week’s mysterious sighting of sewer invaders emerging from a New York City manhole cover, court records revealed on Friday. Samuel Reveron, 25, and Kevin Rodriguez, 26, were each booked on two counts of trespassing. The pair were implicated in the latest sewer incident, in which men were seen climbing out from underground near East 61st Street and Park Avenue at about 1:38 a.m. Wednesday, according to a criminal complaint. At around 4 a.m., “the individuals were observed getting back into the vehicles and driving in tandem over the Queensboro Bridge, alerting the automatic license plate readers as to the vehicle’s’ VIN and license plate numbers,” the complaint said. Reveron and Rodriguez, who own the vehicles, both “identified themselves as the individuals that entered the manhole” early Wednesday morning, according to the court document. They “both described in sum and substance that they entered the manhole together to look for valuables that get washed away in the storm drains and sewers,” authorities said. Reveron and Rodriguez have not been charged in other sewer break-ins, but the NYPD said earlier that Wednesday’s incident “fits that same criteria” previous cases of unauthorized sewer entries. This particular incident raised concerns of local law enforcement, already under strain with the United Nations General Assembly in session and world leaders strolling around New York City. The 61st and Park sighting came steps away from a hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been scheduled to stay. Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, contested allegations his client was in sewers — but said that if his client were underground, there was no intent to injure anyone. “It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News on Friday. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went (into the sewer). But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.” Rodriquez’s attorney declined comment. If it’s proven that Reveron did go underground, Kennedy said he’d counsel his client not to do that again. “It’s not advised to go into a sewer,” Kennedy said. “Besides the grime and rats, there are other dangers down there. It’s not something I would be doing.” Earlier this year, there were at least two incidents of men captured on video mysteriously emerging from New York City sewers. The underground visitors, not affiliated with any public works crews, were seen climbing out of manholes in various Brooklyn neighborhoods in late May. The incidents reignited New York fascination with the urban lore of “mole men” — mythical Big Apple residents who allegedly reside under city streets. The myth was fed a dose of reality in 1993 when late journalist Jennifer Toth published “The Mole People: Life in the Tunnels Beneath New York City,” chronicling homeless people living in or around city train tunnels.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran shows at Gillette Stadium are canceled due to weather
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
articles.body: Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour. The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter, Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement. “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.” The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded. The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views. Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners. Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium. Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest. A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario. “I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.” On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall. The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.

articles.title: IIT Bombay student suicide: Sahil Wakode’s parents spend 8 hours at Crime Branch office amid probe
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The parents of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode, who died by suicide on September 18, spent around eight hours at the Bandra West office of the
articles.body: MUMBAI: The parents of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode, who died by suicide on September 18, spent around eight hours at the Bandra West office of the Mumbai Crime Branch on Friday, an official said.They arrived at 10am and left around 6pm.While their statements had been recorded during an earlier visit, Crime Branch officials did not say whether any additional information or statements were recorded during Friday's session, news agency PTI reported.The Crime Branch has so far recorded statements of 20 people in connection with the case, while efforts are underway to access Wakode's locked mobile phone.Wakode's parents have alleged that their son faced caste discrimination at the institute. They staged a hunger strike at Azad Maidan on Thursday, seeking action against his "tormentors".Union minister of state for social justice and empowerment Ramdas Athawale meanwhile visited IIT Bombay and sought a thorough investigation into Wakode's death, PTI reported.As per the preliminary investigation, Sahil Wakode, 22, a student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, went directly to his hostel room after leaving the examination hall on September 18.The institute had initially said that he was caught using an AI-platform on his mobile phone during the examination. When he did not emerge from his room by around 7pm, the door was opened and he was found dead inside.Among the 20 people questioned so far are students who were present in the examination hall, invigilators and various administrative officials, police said.Wakode's mobile phone was secured with a pattern lock, restricting access, though several missed call notifications were visible on the display screen, a police official said.Forensic experts were trying to access the device, PTI reported.IIT Bombay faculty member Suryanarayan Doolla, who has been named in the police FIR alleging abetment to suicide on grounds of caste discrimination, has been sent on leave to facilitate an impartial probe into the case.Wakode's parents, Ravindra and Sonali Wakode, began a hunger strike at Azad Maidan in Mumbai on Thursday, alleging that their son repeatedly faced caste discrimination at the institute.They left the ground at night.During his visit to IIT Bombay, Athawale, a prominent Dalit leader from Maharashtra, discussed the matter with the institute's director and senior officials. He also visited Wakode's hostel room, officials said."Any student who gets admission to the IIT is very clever and highly capable. Sahil’s death should be thoroughly investigated and action should be taken against those responsible,” the minister said.“The way he died by suicide suggests there could be some major reason behind it. Someone may have insulted him and forced him to take the extreme step,” Athawale said.Athawale said he would discuss the issue with Union education minister Pralhad Joshi, PTI reported.The institute has apologised twice over its earlier communication indicating that Sahil died by suicide hours after allegedly being caught using ChatGPT during an exam.Some TV channels aired CCTV footage from the examination hall showing Sahil's movements before a professor approached him and led him away from the hall.Police said the CCTV footage was being used to reconstruct the sequence of events.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Did Hitler kill his niece?
articles.summary: Newly uncovered archival documents have raised questions over whether Adolf Hitler could have murdered his half-niece, whose death in his Munich apartment in 1931 was officially ruled a suicide.
articles.body: Newly uncovered archival documents have raised questions over whether Adolf Hitler could have murdered his half-niece, whose death in his Munich apartment in 1931 was officially ruled a suicide. Angela ‘Geli’ Raubal, 23, was found dead with a gunshot wound to her chest in Hitler’s Munich apartment in September 1931. The weapon was a pistol belonging to Hitler, who is understood to have had an unusually tight-knit and controlling relationship with his young relative. For 95 years, the accepted account has been that Raubal’s body was discovered on September 19, the date recorded in the Munich police investigation into her death. That morning Georg Winter, Hitler’s personal servant, is understood to have forced open Raubal’s room, which was locked from the inside, and found her body on the floor, according to Munich police records. Official documents show Hitler – who was gaining prominence but had not yet seized power in Germany – had already left Munich for Nuremberg the previous afternoon, a timeline that would prove that he could not have been involved in her death. But German historian Harold Sandner says he has uncovered an entry in Munich’s official death register giving the date and time of the discovery of Raubal’s body as 10.15 a.m. on September 18, 1931. Two death notices found in the archives also carried that date. If those records are authentic, they would place Raubal’s death around 24 hours earlier than previously believed, and put Hitler in Munich when her body was discovered. Official records show he did not leave for Nuremberg until the afternoon of September 18. Sandner has suggested the conflicting records could point to a possible murder cover-up by police officials sympathetic to the Nazi Party. His findings were first published by German news magazine Der Spiegel and will be detailed in his upcoming book, “The Death of Angela ‘Geli’ Raubal: Suicide or Foul Play?” due for publication next month. Thomas Weber, an expert on Nazi Germany and history lecturer at the University of Aberdeen, said Sandner, who he has known for many years, presented his findings to him and that he believes the documents are credible. Describing Sandner as “extremely meticulous and fastidious,” Weber told CNN he initially approached their meeting with skepticism but concluded that the new documents appear to seriously undermine the established chronology of Raubal’s death. “Assuming that the photocopies of the documents that Sandner shared with me are authentic – and I have no reason to doubt that – it seems clear that Raubal died a day earlier than we all have assumed over the last almost one hundred years, and thus that Hitler was still in Munich when she died,” he said. As there are three newly-unearthed documents that put her death as September 18, some sort of clerical error seems unlikely, he added. However, Weber was reluctant to conclude that meant Hitler therefore murdered his niece. He said the Nazis could have had other reasons for wanting to conceal what happened. At the time, the party was seeking mainstream right-wing support, while Hitler was attempting to present himself “for electoral reasons as the embodiment of trust and virtue,” Weber said — something that “any scandal” could have put at risk. A death shrouded in legend Raubal was the daughter of Hitler’s half-sister, Angela Hammitzsch (née Hitler). She lived in her half-uncle’s close proximity for years while her mother served as his housekeeper, before eventually moving into his Munich apartment in 1929. Many historians believe Hitler was infatuated with Raubal and that his behaviour towards her became intensely controlling and possessive in nature. Some have suggested their relationship turned sexual, although this is disputed. He is understood to have exercised considerable control over her life. “The speculation has been that Hitler had an unhealthy obsession with Raubal, that he loved her, and that his interest was incestuous in nature, and that he murdered her out of jealousy because she wanted to leave him, or that he realized that she loved someone else,” Weber said, adding that there were many variations of this speculation. Weber said that while he personally finds it difficult to believe Hitler’s relationship with Raubal was incestuous, his patterns of behaviour certainly suggest he felt a “deep bond” with her. Shortly before her death, Hitler and Raubal are believed to have argued over her desire to leave Munich for Vienna to pursue musical studies. The newly uncovered records do not settle the mystery of how Raubal died. They do, however, reopen questions that have persisted for nearly 100 years about what exactly happened inside his Munich home on the day of her death.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
articles.summary: Israeli PM’s defiant UN speech alienated critics abroad but delighted his base as elections draw near.
articles.body:
In his speech at the United Nations on Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended his country’s genocide in Gaza and its repeated attacks on its neighbours.

Delegates from dozens of countries walked out of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) hall before he spoke, highlighting Israel’s isolation from the rest of the world.

But Netanyahu was appealing to a domestic audience with his speech, a month ahead of critical parliamentary elections that may force him out of office. It was what many Israelis – angry at criticism of their country – want to hear.

In Gaza, Netanyahu said Israel had conducted the “opposite of genocide” – despite the killing of more than 73,000 Palestinians, the destruction of much of Gaza, and the statements from Israeli politicians calling for mass killing in the Palestinian enclave and the removal of its inhabitants.

On the West Bank, the prime minister rejected accusations from Western states that Israel’s occupation was illegitimate, pointing instead to the colonial territories historically held by the United Kingdom and France.

Moreover, despite the public show of criticism, Netanyahu claimed that many of the leaders whose delegates walked out of his speech had privately thanked Israel for “taking out Iran’s nukes”.

And instead of acknowledging that Israel’s actions had organically turned global public opinion against it, he rushed to pin the blame on others.

Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who has been an outspoken critic of Israel, was a “tyrant”, Netanyahu claimed, while Qatar, which has attempted to mediate throughout Israel’s war in Gaza, was accused of funding “toxic media outlets like Al Jazeera”. Israel attacked the Qatari capital Doha in September 2025, before being forced to apologise by US President Donald Trump.

Even the mayor of his host city was not immune from attack, with Netanyahu branding New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani an antiSemite and claiming that, despite the large number of Jewish groups protesting his presence outside the UN building, Jews were being “demonised” in New York.

Hamad AlMuftah, deputy chief of mission at the Qatari Embassy in Washington, responded to Netanyahu’s claims, referencing the walkout in the hall and highlighting his country’s role as a regional mediator.

“At a moment of profound regional and domestic political turmoil, attacking one of the countries doing the difficult work of mediation does nothing to solve the problem,” he said.

Turkiye and Mamdani were also emphatic in rejecting Netanyahu’s accusations. Turkiye’s presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran described Netanyahu’s remarks as baseless. He argued they were unlikely to distract from either Israel’s ongoing attacks in Gaza, where it continues to kill Palestinians in defiance of a so-called “ceasefire”, or the International Criminal Court proceedings against Netanyahu.

Mamdani likewise referenced the ICC warrant issued for Netanyahu for the war crimes he is alleged to have overseen in Gaza and the “baseless lies” intended to “sanitise his genocide of Palestinians”.

“Netanyahu’s speech was meant to boost his election campaign back at home,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “His supporters loved it. Those who don’t support him could see in his speech the classic Netanyahu – brilliant orator but a serial liar.”

“His speech was littered with lies,” Bregman continued. “He played down the settlers’s violence in the West Bank, saying that just a few Palestinians were killed by it, while in reality more than 80 were killed [by Israeli forces and settlers] there this year.”

“The world has turned its back on him and on Israel,” Bregman added. “He’s toxic, and Israel has turned itself into a pariah state.”

However, while Netanyahu may have faced growing international isolation, his allies in the Israeli government and some media outlets rallied around what they portrayed as the defiant tone of his speech.

Zvika Klein, editor of the influential right-wing newspaper the Jerusalem Post, praised Netanyahu’s delivery and defence of Israel. Columnists in other Israeli media also rushed to compare Netanyahu’s warnings to the West to that of a stern father addressing a wayward son.

“He gave a great performance,” said Mitchell Barak, an Israeli pollster and former aide to Netanyahu during the 1990s.

Barak argued that the speech was designed to leave the delegates who stayed with the impression that Israel’s wars since 2023 had been fought not only in its own interests, but also on behalf of its allies and the wider international community.

“No one watching in Israel could imagine any of Netanyahu’s [electoral] rivals in October doing that. It’s impossible to picture it. None of them could have commanded that much respect,” he claimed.

While much of Netanyahu’s electoral base may have been reassured by his address, nowhere in his speech was any hint of where Israel’s multiple wars and genocide might end.

For three years, he boasted, Israel had fought on seven fronts.

As it led a genocide in Gaza, Israel has also battled Hezbollah, Yemen’s Houthi rebels, Iran, militias in Iraq and Syria as well as Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. All, he claimed, had “ganged up” to wipe Israel “off the face of the Earth”.

Closing his speech, Netanyahu addressed the remaining delegates as one, maintaining: “Over the centuries, the tyrannies that tried to destroy us failed time and again. God willing, they’ll continue to fail. If we muster our courage, if we steel our resolve, we will continue to win.”

“This was just a repeat of his Sparta speech,“ Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with Chatham House said, referring to Netanyahu’s likening of Israel in September 2025 to the ancient and perennially embattled city-state.

“All he could offer was repeated references to his past heroism, military success and the need to keep fighting. That’s something that should be of concern to every Israeli watching,” Mekelberg said.

“Where does this end? There’s no answer; there isn’t even the vocabulary for that. When Israel’s leaders have no solution to the country’s multiple wars, that’s when every Israeli should be worried.”

articles.title: Ed Sheeran concerts at Robert Kraft stadiums cancelled over weather
articles.summary: Singer’s tour has faced numerous setbacks after expulsion of rapper Macklemore over support for Palestine drew backlash.
articles.body:
Ed Sheeran’s tour of the United States has been dealt another setback, with shows scheduled to take place in the stadium owned by pro-Israel billionaire Robert Kraft cancelled due to bad weather.

Gillette Stadium in the state of Massachusetts announced that shows scheduled for Friday and Saturday have been cancelled in anticipation of a major storm expected to bring heavy rainfall. The news was first reported by the outlet TMZ.

“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the venue said in a statement on Friday.

“The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”

The stadium said tickets are refundable and that Ticketmaster ticketholders would receive automatic refunds.

Kraft played a key role in the expulsion earlier this month of the rapper Macklemore , Sheeran’s opening act for his US leg of the concert and an outspoken critic of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Macklemore was dropped for yelling “Free Palestine” on stage during a show in New Jersey, sparking a strong backlash with many concertgoers choosing to boycott it instead.

The controversy came to represent the substantial influence wielded by pro-Israel figures, but also underscored a massive shift in public opinion away from support for Israel that has taken place in the US over the last several years.

Amid public outcry, many artists scheduled to play with Sheeran on the tour announced they would drop out in solidarity with Macklemore. Newsweek reported that ticket prices for Sheeran’s concerts have fallen by more than 10 percent in recent days, citing TicketData.

Macklemore announced a tour of his own in support of Palestine earlier this week, stating that the proceeds will go towards organisations that help the Palestinians.

“Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” he said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it.”

articles.title: Trump's quiet China wins are more important than Xi's empty state visit
articles.summary: The U.S.-China trade deficit is falling fast, but Xi Jinping offered little beyond pandas and ping-pong diplomacy during Trump's State Visit.
articles.body: China’s President Xi Jinping, ruler for life, is not ready to make sweeping deals with the USA on soybeans, AI or anything else. This was a State Visit, not a summit, but even so, deliverables were light. China’s state-owned People’s Daily was so strapped for material that they ran a story titled: "Bonded by Ping-Pong: China-U.S. friendship writes a new chapter." But don’t lose heart. The Trump Administration has scored some quiet wins and much better field position for the long haul. "The old adage of deliverables in a relationship that we have with China is really not measurable in many ways," said U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue. It’s about "continuing the conversation." What matters most to America in the long term is the trade deficit. Good news: it's falling. Already the gap between U.S. exports and imports from China is down from $297 billion in 2024 to $202 billion in 2025, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says the deficit is on track to drop to $140 billion for 2026. If achieved, this is a historic reversal of globalization. The gap hasn’t been this low in over 20 years. TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING Credit what Team Trump calls "managed" trade: specific, non-sensitive goods, such as agricultural products and medical devices. "All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer told CNBC. Greer promised more trade details next week. However, China has bought only half the amount of soybeans agreed, according to American Soybean Association President Scott Metzger, so there’s still a ways to go on the trade balance. This is not glamorous work. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent held a 12-hour meeting on Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. In the end, all the two sides could do was extend the 2025 truce for two more months. You remember what happened last year: China stopped licensing rare earth material exports, and Trump slapped on massive tariffs. "I don’t know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don’t know whether we will just roll the current deal," Bessent said Wednesday. The Bessent-He meeting was also supposed to tee up some kind of agreement on an artificial intelligence safety mechanism for Trump and Xi. Afterwards, Bessent kept to the optimistic line that China was eager to engage, and spoke about at least setting up a hot line to deal with incidents across borders. Don’t count on much more. China does not participate in nuclear arms control. Any AI accord will be all talk with no teeth, just like the U.S.-China fentanyl working group. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD What’s much more important is keeping the U.S. AI tech stack ahead of China. At the White House State Dinner on Thursday night, it was good to see Trump assemble the tech titans as he did on his visit to Beijing in May. These leaders from Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Google, Dell, OpenAI, Citigroup, etc. have the cash and the smarts to keep the U.S. in the lead in AI. SpaceX and Amazon Leo are launching satellites that will keep U.S. dominance over China in the low earth orbit market sector. Google has Project Suncatcher to try running its tensor processing units with solar power on orbit. Innovation is America’s edge over China. Yes, they'd like to book deals with China in areas such as chips and financial services, but China has been lagging. For example, Nvidia is cleared to sell its H200 chips to China (not its most advanced products) but only small batches of chips have been purchased by Tencent and ByteDance. The reality is that China is cutting imports under Xi’s policy of semi-conductor self-reliance. That’s a sign that China is girding for long-term conflict. Fortunately, President Trump has taken many actions to strengthen America’s position. The Greenland agreement, investing in Venezuela’s oil, getting Chinese operators out of the Panama Canal Zone, a hefty defense budget aimed at countering China, expanding the Space Force, and yes, the U.S. Navy blockade of the Strait of Hormuz: all this has protected American interests. Boundaries are good for geopolitics. CHINA IS TAKING THE FIGHT TO THE STARS. AMERICA MUST RECLAIM SPACE SUPREMACY And what did Xi contribute? Xi Jinping announced China’s welcome loan of two pandas to the Atlanta Zoo, and a preposterous initiative for 100,000 Americans to study in China over the next five years. This, from a China ramping up nuclear weapons production, hassling U.S. satellites on orbit, backing Russia with oil purchases and defense electronics, and giving what Perdue termed "intel and parts" to Iran. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That offer was deeply cynical. Xi wants to show off Chinese culture, but in fact, there are fewer than 2,000 American students in China compared to 265,919 Chinese students in the USA. Last fall, Harvard enrolled 1,452 students from China, mostly graduate students. But if you want to go, Duke University has a joint venture in China which got a flattering and no doubt coincidental write-up in the state-owned China Daily on Friday.

articles.title: Man arrested six years after his wife’s remains were found in a crawlspace
articles.summary: A man in Southern California is facing murder charges in connection to his wife’s killing 20 years ago.
articles.body: A man in Southern California is facing murder charges in connection to his wife’s killing 20 years ago. Jeff Anthony Maiorca, 53, was arrested Monday after local authorities in San Bernardino discovered the remains of Jill Maiorca hidden in the crawlspace beneath a home in Big Bear. Jill Maiorca was reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007 and authorities now say she was murdered in November 2006, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. She was 29. Authorities resumed their investigation into her disappearance on Oct. 28, 2020, when deputies from the Big Bear Sheriff’s Station responded to a call from someone who reported “a suspicious discovery in the crawlspace” under a residence, the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department said in a news release on Monday night. Upon arrival, they realize that hidden beneath the home were “unidentified human remains.” An autopsy conducted on the remains determined the manner of death to be homicide. In 2023, the remains were identified as those of Jill Maiorca following “additional investigative DNA analysis” after cold case homicide investigators took over the case, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. Her remains had long been concealed beneath the Big Bear house without the homeowner’s knowledge. Cold case detectives eventually identified Jill Maiorca’s former husband, Jeff Maiorca, as a suspect in her murder. Public records show Jeff Maiorca had filed for divorce from Jill Maiorca in Los Angeles County in 2004. Local authorities detained Jeff Maiorca on Monday afternoon at the Big Bear Lake branch library on Garstin Drive, arrest records show. He is currently being held without bail at the High Desert Jail in Adelanto, California. Records from the San Bernardino County Superior Court in California show Jeff Maiorca had an initial hearing on Wednesday. He was formally charged with murder and use of a deadly weapon, records show. Records do not yet list an attorney for Jeff Maiorca. His next court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 12. The investigation into Jill Maiorca’s disappearance and death remain ongoing. The San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department is encouraging anyone with information to contact their homicide detail team.

articles.title: Zelensky says Russia has widened attacks to hit Ukraine's data centres and internet providers
articles.summary: Such strikes aim to disrupt "people's ability to stay connected, study, work", says Ukraine's president.
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people.

"All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.

On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said the teenager was an Israeli citizen.

Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes. Some firms are already transferring data from damaged servers abroad.

In the north-western city Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".

In a post on social media on Friday, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers - for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target.

"It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."

On Wednesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres.

"Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.

Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.

But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access".

The latest data centre hit by Russia is run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after Friday's daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites".

Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence.

Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC.

The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi.

In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure - seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches.

Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In a separate development on Friday, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday.

In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented.

The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.

In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.

articles.title: Andy Burnham rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers
articles.summary: Andy Burnham told the BBC Westminster should have a “say on an issue of that magnitude”.
articles.body:
The prime minister has ruled out handing powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government.

Andy Burnham said other UK nations do not have such powers and he did not "think we can create a different arrangement for Wales".

He added that the decision should be made jointly with Westminster, arguing that the UK Parliament has to have a "say on an issue of that magnitude".

Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said last week he would seek powers to hold an independence referendum, although he ruled out staging one before the next Senedd election in May 2030.

Burnham also said he was open to looking at the Welsh government's "Cynnal" plans to trial offering £10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six , in households already receiving universal credit.

This would require the agreement of the Department for Work and Pensions and HMRC to avoid the payment being taxed or other benefits - paid for by the UK government - being reduced.

"I'll certainly ensure that there's a proper discussion about the issue," he said.

"I mean, I did things as mayor of Greater Manchester without there having to be any tax implications.

"So I'm not quite sure why that arises in this in this instance, but we will have a look at it for certain."

During a visit to the Tata steelworks in Port Talbot in August, Burnham indicated he was "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing .

BBC Wales understands that idea faces oppostion from many Welsh Labour MPs, with one calling it "a travesty".

In response Burnham said on Friday it was "about looking at the case" rather than taking "a fixed view".

He added: "I just need to look at it on the merits of the case. I'm the prime minister of all of the UK, including Wales.

"I have to respect the governments in the the nations of the UK, and I will, and give fair hearing to anything that is is put to me."

Labour's conference will get underway with renewed debate about Wales' constitutional future and whether further powers should be devolved to Cardiff Bay from Westminster.

Earlier this week a Reform motion that Wales should remain as part of the UK was voted down by the Senedd.

A revised Plaid Cymru motion that the people of Wales should decide Wales's constitutional future was passed.

Last week, the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff and signed an agreement stating that Westminster should not undermine the right of the people in their nations to decide their own future.

Burnham will address his first Labour conference as Prime Minister next week and is expected to set out his vision for the UK for the next 10 years.

The conversations about devolution, powers and funding will not stop after this weekend.

Next month the prime minister is scheduled to meet first ministers from all the nations of the UK.
